blocks.text: 1. overview

blocks.alt: Correct predictions over total predictions gives accuracy

blocks.text: The Model Evaluation Regression module, just completed, built a full toolkit for measuring how far a continuous numeric prediction lands from its true value. The Model Evaluation Classification module now turns to the discrete side of prediction, covered throughout the entire Classification Algorithms module, Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest, and every boosting method, and Accuracy is the simplest, most intuitive place to begin: what fraction of a model's predictions were exactly correct?

Accuracy has an immediate, universal appeal, since it maps directly onto how most people already think about correctness in everyday life, get it right or get it wrong, count up the right ones, divide by the total. This topic covers accuracy's formula in full, but spends real, deliberate time on its most important, most consequential limitation, one that makes it a genuinely dangerous metric to rely on blindly in a specific, common situation covered in depth later in this topic.
2. The Formula

blocks.alt: Correct predictions divided by all predictions gives accuracy

blocks.text: Accuracy is computed in the most direct way imaginable: count every single prediction a model makes that exactly matches the true label, then divide that count by the total number of predictions made across the entire evaluation dataset. The resulting number always falls between 0 and 1, and it is very often reported instead as an equivalent percentage, an accuracy of 0.92 being reported as 92 percent correct.

This simplicity is genuinely part of accuracy's appeal: unlike several metrics covered later in this module, there is no transformation, no weighting, and no separate calculation required to understand what the number actually means. An accuracy of 92 percent means exactly what it sounds like, 92 out of every 100 predictions, on average, were exactly right.
3. A Preview of the Confusion Matrix

Every single prediction a binary classifier makes falls into exactly one of four categories, a framework covered in its own full, dedicated depth in the Confusion Matrix topic later in this module, but worth previewing briefly here since accuracy is built directly from it. A True Positive is a case where the model predicted positive and the true label actually was positive. A True Negative is a case where the model predicted negative and the true label actually was negative.

A False Positive is a case where the model predicted positive but the true label was actually negative, and a False Negative is a case where the model predicted negative but the true label was actually positive. Accuracy, expressed in terms of these four categories, is simply the count of True Positives plus True Negatives, divided by the total count across all four categories combined, a framing that becomes essential for understanding Precision and Recall, covered in the next two topics.

blocks.text: 4. Accuracy's Critical Weakness: Class Imbalance

blocks.alt: 99 percent majority class gives high accuracy that is meaningless

blocks.text: The Handling Imbalanced Data module, covered earlier in this course, established that many real-world classification problems have a heavily skewed class distribution, one class vastly outnumbering the other, fraud detection, rare disease diagnosis, and manufacturing defect detection all being classic examples. Accuracy interacts with this exact situation in a genuinely dangerous, deceptive way.

Consider a dataset where 99 percent of examples belong to the negative class and only 1 percent belong to the positive class, a realistic proportion for something like rare disease detection. A trivial model that simply predicts negative for every single example, completely ignoring every input feature, achieves 99 percent accuracy on this dataset, despite catching precisely zero of the actual positive cases, the exact cases the model presumably exists to detect in the first place. This is not a hypothetical edge case; it is one of the most common, consequential pitfalls in all of applied classification.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Whenever accuracy is reported for a classification problem, the class distribution should be checked immediately alongside it. A high accuracy on a heavily imbalanced dataset proves almost nothing about whether the model actually learned to detect the minority class at all.

blocks.text: 5. Judging Accuracy Against a Majority-Class Baseline

blocks.alt: Model accuracy is judged against a majority class baseline

blocks.text: This connects directly back to the naive-baseline comparison technique already introduced for regression metrics in the MAE topic of the previous module. For classification, the equivalent naive baseline is a model that always predicts whichever class is most common in the dataset, the majority class, regardless of the actual input features.

This naive baseline's accuracy is always exactly equal to the majority class's share of the total dataset, 99 percent in the rare-disease example covered in the previous section. Any real, properly trained model needs to clear this baseline meaningfully, not just barely, to demonstrate it has genuinely learned something useful about the relationship between features and class label, exactly the same principle already established for regression metrics, now applied directly to classification.
6. When Accuracy Is a Trustworthy Metric

Despite its serious weakness on imbalanced data, accuracy remains a genuinely reasonable, trustworthy metric in the right circumstances. It works well whenever the classes in a dataset are roughly balanced, meaning no single class dominates the count of examples, since in that situation a trivial majority-class model provides little advantage and a genuinely high accuracy score does reflect real, meaningful predictive skill.

It also works well whenever every kind of classification error is roughly equally costly, meaning there is no strong reason to weigh a false positive differently from a false negative in terms of real-world consequence, a situation where accuracy's treatment of every error identically is entirely appropriate rather than a genuine blind spot. Recognizing whether a given problem actually satisfies both of these conditions is the key judgment call before trusting accuracy as the primary evaluation metric.

blocks.text: 7. Accuracy Beyond Binary Classification

Every classification example covered so far in this topic has involved binary classification, exactly two possible classes, positive or negative. Accuracy generalizes directly and naturally to multiclass classification, problems with three or more possible classes, exactly the setting already covered for the One-vs-Rest and softmax extensions of Logistic Regression back in the Classification module, digit recognition with ten possible classes being a classic example.

The formula stays exactly the same: count every prediction that exactly matches its true label, across every class simultaneously, and divide by the total number of predictions. Class imbalance remains just as real a risk in the multiclass setting, now potentially spread across several classes of very different sizes rather than just two, and the same majority-baseline comparison technique covered in the previous section applies equally well here, comparing against whichever single class happens to be most common overall.
8. Balanced Accuracy: A Direct Fix

blocks.alt: Plain accuracy gets fixed directly by balanced accuracy

blocks.text: Plain accuracy, as covered throughout this topic, weighs every individual prediction identically, which is precisely the mechanism through which a large majority class can dominate the overall score. Balanced Accuracy offers a direct, practical fix without abandoning the accuracy concept entirely: rather than averaging correctness across every individual prediction, it first computes accuracy separately within each class, then averages those per-class accuracy values together.

This prevents a large majority class from completely dominating the overall reported score, since each class, regardless of how many examples it actually contains, contributes equally to the final averaged result. On the rare-disease example covered earlier in this topic, a trivial always-predict-negative model would score 100 percent accuracy on the negative class but 0 percent accuracy on the positive class, and Balanced Accuracy would average these to 50 percent, honestly reflecting the model's complete failure to detect the minority class, in sharp contrast to plain accuracy's misleadingly high 99 percent.

blocks.title: tip
blocks.content: Balanced Accuracy is a genuinely useful, quick fix when a single summary number is still wanted despite known class imbalance, though Precision, Recall, and F1 Score, covered in the next three topics, generally offer an even richer, more actionable picture of exactly where a model succeeds and fails.

blocks.text: 9. Summarizing Accuracy's Core Limitation

It is worth stating plainly, before moving to the next topic, exactly what accuracy cannot tell you. Its most serious weakness, covered in depth earlier in this topic, is class imbalance: a trivial, majority-class-only model can achieve a deceptively high accuracy score while providing zero real value for the minority class it presumably exists to detect.

Its second, related weakness is that it treats every kind of error identically, with no way to distinguish a costly false negative, missing a genuine fraud case or a real disease diagnosis, from a comparatively harmless false positive, flagging a legitimate transaction for extra review. Precision and Recall, the next two topics in this module, exist specifically to address these two exact blind spots, breaking classification performance apart into pieces that reveal exactly where, and in which direction, a model's errors actually occur.
10. Worked Example
The example below computes plain accuracy and Balanced Accuracy on a deliberately imbalanced dataset, directly illustrating how differently the two metrics judge a trivial majority-class model.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, balanced_accuracy_score
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)

# A heavily imbalanced dataset: 99% negative class, 1% positive class
X_majority = rng.normal(loc=[0, 0], scale=1, size=(990, 2))
X_minority = rng.normal(loc=[5, 5], scale=1, size=(10, 2))
X = np.vstack([X_majority, X_minority])
y = np.array([0] * 990 + [1] * 10)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=y)

# A trivial baseline that always predicts the majority class
dummy = DummyClassifier(strategy='most_frequent')
dummy.fit(X_train, y_train)
dummy_predictions = dummy.predict(X_test)

# A genuinely trained model
model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
model_predictions = model.predict(X_test)

for name, predictions in [("Trivial majority-class model", dummy_predictions), ("Trained Logistic Regression", model_predictions)]:
    acc = accuracy_score(y_test, predictions)
    bal_acc = balanced_accuracy_score(y_test, predictions)
    print(f"{name}: accuracy={acc:.3f}, balanced_accuracy={bal_acc:.3f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Run this and compare the two trivial-model scores directly: plain accuracy looks deceptively strong, close to 99 percent, while Balanced Accuracy honestly reveals the trivial model's complete failure to detect the minority class, close to 50 percent, exactly the contrast covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Accuracy divides the count of correct predictions by the total number of predictions, the simplest classification metric.
It is built from the four confusion matrix categories: True Positive, True Negative, False Positive, and False Negative.
On heavily imbalanced data, a trivial majority-class model can achieve deceptively high accuracy while catching zero minority-class cases.
Comparing against a majority-class baseline gives accuracy real, judgable context, echoing the naive-baseline technique from regression metrics.
Accuracy is trustworthy specifically when classes are roughly balanced and every kind of error carries roughly equal cost.
It generalizes directly to multiclass problems, with the same formula and the same imbalance risk.
Balanced Accuracy averages per-class accuracy, directly fixing the majority-class-domination problem without abandoning the metric.
Accuracy cannot distinguish a costly error from a harmless one, treating every kind of mistake identically.
Next up: Precision, which asks a sharper question: of everything the model predicted positive, how many actually were?
